title: Spot the bug
prompt:
What happens when you call `f(3)`?
`public int f(int n) { return n + f(n - 1); }`
options: StackOverflowError — there's no base case, so it recurses forever
explanation: Nothing ever stops the recursion: f(3) → f(2) → f(1) → f(0) → f(-1) → ... until the call stack runs out. Base case first, always.

title: Fibonacci skeleton
prompt: Complete the classic (inefficient but canonical) recursive Fibonacci.
explanation: fib(0)=0 and fib(1)=1, which `return n` covers in one line. Each call branches into two — that exponential blowup is exactly what memoization fixes next.

title: Predict the output: counting calls
prompt: `demo()` is called on a fresh `Solution`. How many times does `fib` run in total? (The tree above shows `fib(4)` makes 9 calls.)
explanation: calls(n) = 1 + calls(n-1) + calls(n-2), with calls(0) = calls(1) = 1. So calls(2) = 3, calls(3) = 5, calls(4) = 9, and calls(5) = 1 + 9 + 5 = 15. The count grows almost as fast as Fibonacci itself — that's the exponential blowup.

title: Fibonacci with memoization
prompt: Return the n-th Fibonacci number (`fib(0) = 0`, `fib(1) = 1`) for `0 ≤ n ≤ 50`. Plain recursion is far too slow for n = 50 — use a `long[] memo` passed to a recursive helper. The result needs `long`.

tests.note: too slow without memo; needs long

solution.explanation: Each `fibMemo(k)` computes its value once and stores it; every later request is an O(1) lookup. That cuts the call tree from O(2ⁿ) to O(n) time, with O(n) memo space and recursion depth. `-1` is a safe 'not computed' marker because Fibonacci values are never negative.

hints: The slow part is solving the same `fib(k)` over and over — store each answer the first time.
Make a `long[] memo` of size `n + 1`, fill it with `-1`, and pass it to a private recursive helper.
In the helper, after the base case: `if (memo[n] != -1) return memo[n];` — otherwise compute, store in `memo[n]`, and return it.

title: Recursive array sum with a helper
prompt: Return the sum of `nums` recursively — no loops. The given signature has no index, so write a private helper `sumFrom(int[] nums, int i)` that returns the sum of `nums[i..end]`, and call it with `i = 0`.

solution.explanation: The helper's extra parameter `i` tracks where the unsolved part starts. Base case: past the end, the sum is 0. Otherwise take `nums[i]` and trust the call for the rest. O(n) time and O(n) stack depth.

hints: The public method can't say 'the rest of the array' — a helper with an index can.
Base case: when `i == nums.length`, there's nothing left to add.
Recursive case: `nums[i] + sumFrom(nums, i + 1)`; the public method just returns `sumFrom(nums, 0)`.

title: Power, recursively
prompt: Return `base` raised to `exp` (exp ≥ 0) using recursion, not `Math.pow`. Base case: anything to the 0th power is 1. Recursive case: `base * power(base, exp - 1)`.

solution.explanation: The return type is `long` because 2^40 overflows int; since `power(...)` returns a long, `base * power(...)` multiplies in long. O(exp) calls. (Fast exponentiation halves exp instead — an optimization you'll meet later.)

hints: Which exponent has an answer you know without any work? That's your base case.

title: Drill: recursive digit count
prompt: From memory: return the number of digits in `n` (n ≥ 0) recursively. Base case: `n < 10` has 1 digit. Otherwise: 1 + digits of `n / 10`.

solution.explanation: `n / 10` drops one digit, so each call counts one and recurses on the rest. The base case `n < 10` covers 0-9 (including 0, which has one digit). O(number of digits).

hints: Which inputs obviously have exactly one digit? Stop there.
Base case handles 0-9 in one line: `if (n < 10) return 1;`
Otherwise count this digit and recurse on `n / 10`.
